papers.title: Computational Process Modeling for Additive Manufacturing (OSU)
papers.abstract: Powder-Bed Additive Manufacturing (AM) through Direct Metal Laser Sintering (DMLS) or Selective Laser Melting (SLM) is being used by NASA and the Aerospace industry to parts that traditionally are very complex, high cost, or long schedule lead items. The process spreads a thin layer of metal powder over a build platform, then melts the powder in a series of welds in a desired shape. The next layer of powder is applied, and the process is repeated until layer-by-layer, a very complex part can be built. This reduces cost and schedule by eliminating very complex tooling and processes traditionally used in aerospace component manufacturing. To use the process to print end-use items, NASA seeks to understand SLM material well enough to develop a method of qualifying parts for space flight operation. Traditionally, a new material process takes many years and high investment to generate statistical databases and experiential knowledge, but computational modeling can truncate the schedule and cost -many experiments can be run quickly in a model, which would take years and a high material cost to run empirically. This project seeks to optimize material build parameters with reduced time and cost through modeling.

summary_en.motivation: To reduce time and cost of qualifying additive manufacturing parts through computational modeling instead of extensive empirical testing.
summary_en.method: Computational process models are developed to simulate powder-bed fusion (SLM/DMLS) and optimize build parameters.
summary_en.result: The modeling approach aims to accelerate process parameter optimization and reduce experimental burden.
summary_en.validation: No experimental validation is reported; the work is a project overview with proposed modeling methodology.
